chapters.category: Aramaic, Greek and Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 29 — Trees of Frankincense and Myrrh
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest primary-language witnesses available for this chapter. The extant Aramaic of 4Q206 (4QEnoch e) preserves and governs both verses, including the eastern wooded place, the fragrant substances frankincense and myrrh, and the comparison with almond trees. The Greek Codex Panopolitanus (Cairo Papyrus 10759) independently preserves the complete two-verse chapter and confirms its sequence. The aromatic-tree wording is rendered without assigning a botanical species beyond the ancient comparison. No unattested wording was supplied, and no modern English translation was used as the translation base.

verses.text: From there I journeyed to another place and saw, east of this mountain, a wooded region.
verses.study: Enoch continues eastward from the watered wilderness into a distinct forested place. The brief transition locates the trees before describing their fragrance. The landscape is not empty scenery; each stage discloses another ordered provision within creation.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:8 — God plants a garden toward the east
Psalm 104:16 — the trees of the LORD are richly supplied
Isaiah 41:19 — diverse trees are placed in the wilderness
1 Enoch 28:1–3 — the preceding wilderness contains trees, abundant water and dew

verses.text: There I saw aromatic trees breathing out the fragrances of frankincense and myrrh, and the trees were like almond trees.
verses.study: The forest is identified by scent as well as sight. Frankincense and myrrh belong to valued aromatic use in biblical worship, anointing and burial, while the almond-tree comparison describes the trees' appearance without claiming a precise modern species. The vision honors created fragrance without turning the trees themselves into objects of worship.
crossReferences: Exodus 30:23–25, 34–38 — myrrh and frankincense are used in holy anointing oil and incense
Numbers 17:8 — Aaron's almond staff buds, blossoms and bears fruit
Song of Songs 4:6, 14 — myrrh and frankincense mark a fragrant garden
Matthew 2:11 — frankincense and myrrh are presented among precious gifts

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 29 condenses its vision into two senses: Enoch sees a wooded eastern place and smells trees exhaling frankincense and myrrh. The almond-tree comparison gives the aromatic grove a familiar visible form while leaving its exact species unnamed.

The chapter continues the movement from wilderness abundance into increasingly precious created gifts. Water and dew sustain the landscape of Chapter 28; Chapter 29 adds fragrance associated elsewhere in Scripture with consecration, prayer, royal gift and burial.

These biblical connections enrich the imagery but do not change the chapter into a ritual instruction. Enoch is observing what exists in the visionary landscape, not commanding readers to reproduce its substances or worship its trees.

The early Aramaic survival is especially valuable here because it confirms both verses and clarifies the aromatic wording where the later Greek text is difficult. The chapter can therefore be translated without supplying a speculative plant name.

crossReferences: Exodus 30:23–38 — myrrh and frankincense in consecrated oil and incense
Numbers 17:8 — the blossoming and fruit-bearing almond staff
Song of Songs 4:6, 14 — a garden fragrant with myrrh and frankincense
Matthew 2:11; John 19:39 — precious aromatics at Jesus' birth and burial
